Given your context — healthcare, PHI, hybrid infra, cloud EHR, ITIL already in place — here's a realistic prioritized checklist. I've structured it as three phases that fit a 6–9 month runway, with the quick wins front-loaded.

---

# ISO 27001:2022 Gap Analysis Checklist
### Healthcare Provider | 250 staff | Hybrid cloud | PHI in scope

---

## How to read this

**Gap severity** = H (likely missing/critical), M (partial), L (probably exists, needs documenting).
**Evidence** = what an auditor will actually ask to see, not just "a policy exists."

---

## Phase 1: Foundation (Months 1–2) — Quick Wins + Mandatory Clause Work

These are either fast to complete or mandatory before anything else can be assessed. Auditors look here first.

---

### Clause 4–6: Context, Leadership, Risk (Mandatory clauses — not Annex A)

These are **not optional**. No certificate without them.

| # | Requirement | Gap | Actions | Auditor evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Scope statement (4.3) | H | Define ISMS boundary: include cloud EHR, on-prem, staff devices, third-party connections. Be specific about PHI systems. | Signed, dated scope document referencing systems and locations |
| 2 | Context and interested parties (4.1–4.2) | H | Document internal/external issues (HIPAA, state regs, payer requirements, cyber insurers). List stakeholders and their requirements. | Context register or equivalent document |
| 3 | Information security policy (5.2) | M | You likely have fragments. Consolidate into a top-level IS policy signed by CEO/COO. One page is fine. | Signed policy, evidence of communication to all staff |
| 4 | Risk assessment methodology (6.1.2) | H | Define how you assess risk before you assess anything. Choose asset-based or scenario-based. Document criteria for likelihood, impact, and risk acceptance. | Risk methodology document, approved by leadership |
| 5 | Statement of Applicability (6.1.3) | H | List all 93 Annex A controls, justify inclusions/exclusions. This is the central audit artifact. | Completed SoA with justification column and control owner for each included control |
| 6 | Risk treatment plan (6.1.3) | H | Assign owners, timelines, and treatment decisions (accept/mitigate/transfer) to each identified risk. | Risk register with treatment decisions, risk owner signatures |

---

### Annex A Quick Wins — High impact, low effort given your ITIL baseline

**A.5.1 — Policies for information security**

| Gap | Action | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| M — fragments exist | Consolidate into a policy suite: IS policy, acceptable use, access control, remote work, BYOD, PHI handling. Publish on intranet. | Policy documents, version control history, staff acknowledgment records |

**A.6.3 — Information security awareness and training**

| Gap | Action | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| M | Run a mandatory annual security awareness session. Healthcare staff are often already doing HIPAA training — map it. Record completion. | Training completion records, training content, dates, sign-off or LMS export |

**A.5.9 — Inventory of information and assets**

| Gap | Action | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| H | Build an asset register covering hardware, software, cloud services, data flows (especially PHI). Your ITIL CMDB is a starting point but likely needs PHI classification added. | Asset register with owner, classification (confidential/PHI/public), and location columns |

**A.5.12 / 5.13 — Classification and labeling**

| Gap | Action | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| H in healthcare | Define at minimum: Public, Internal, Confidential, PHI/Restricted. Apply to documents and data stores. | Classification scheme document, examples of labeled assets, policy |

**A.8.9 — Configuration management** *(quick win if ITIL CMDB exists)*

| Gap | Action | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| M | Extend your CMDB to include security-relevant configs (firewall rules, cloud security group settings, EHR access configs). | CMDB export, configuration baseline documents |

---

## Phase 2: Core Controls (Months 2–5) — The Heavy Lifting

This is where most of the gap will be in a no-formal-ISMS environment. Tackle in roughly this order.

---

### Access Control — Annex A 5.15–5.18, 8.2, 8.3

This is the highest-risk area for a healthcare provider with PHI and will get the most auditor scrutiny.

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.15 Access control policy | H | Write a formal access control policy covering role-based access, least privilege, and PHI access rules. | Signed policy, review date |
| 5.16 Identity management | M | Confirm all accounts are linked to named individuals. No shared accounts for PHI systems. Document process for joiner/mover/leaver. | Identity management procedure, HR-to-IT onboarding/offboarding workflow |
| 5.17 Authentication | M | MFA mandatory for cloud EHR, remote access, admin accounts. Document where it's enforced. | MFA configuration screenshots, policy, any exemption register |
| 5.18 Access rights review | H | Run a formal access rights review (quarterly recommended for PHI). Document results and any remediation. | Access review records, sign-off by system owners, evidence of revocations actioned |
| 8.2 Privileged access | H | Inventory all privileged accounts (local admin, cloud IAM admin, EHR admin). Apply just-in-time or time-limited access where feasible. | Privileged account register, PAM controls documented |
| 8.3 Information access restriction | M | Confirm EHR access is restricted by role/need. Document who approved what access. | Role-based access matrix, approval records |

---

### Cryptography — A.8.24

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.24 Use of cryptography | M–H | Document encryption in use: EHR data at rest and in transit, laptop encryption, backup encryption. Confirm TLS versions, key management. | Cryptography policy, encryption configuration evidence (screenshots or config extracts), key management procedure |

This is a HIPAA technical safeguard as well, so you likely have some of this documented already.

---

### Physical and Environmental — A.7.1–7.14

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1–7.4 Physical security | M | On-prem server room: document access controls (key card, log), clean desk policy, visitor management. Cloud: document that physical security is handled by provider (AWS/Azure BAA and SOC 2 report covers this). | Physical access logs, clean desk policy, cloud provider security documentation |
| 7.14 Secure disposal | H | Document process for wiping/destroying devices. Healthcare PHI makes this a HIPAA requirement too. | Disposal procedure, certificate of destruction records |

---

### Supplier and Cloud Provider Management — A.5.19–5.23

Critical for your environment given cloud-hosted EHR and hybrid infra.

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.19 Supplier security policy | H | Write a supplier information security policy. Identify all suppliers with access to PHI or infrastructure. | Policy document, supplier register |
| 5.20 Addressing security in supplier agreements | H | Confirm BAA exists with EHR vendor. Review contracts for security clauses (incident notification, audit rights, sub-processor disclosure). | BAA copies, contract clauses, supplier security questionnaires |
| 5.21–5.22 Supply chain, monitoring | M | Annual review of key supplier security posture. Request SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certs from EHR vendor and cloud provider. | Supplier review records, certificates received |
| 5.23 Cloud services security | H | Document your shared responsibility model for each cloud service. What does the provider own vs. what do you own? | Shared responsibility matrix per cloud service, cloud provider security documentation |

---

### Vulnerability and Patch Management — A.8.8

This is your most significant technical gap based on your description.

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.8 Technical vulnerability management | H | Implement a formal patching process: scan, assess, prioritize (CVSS + asset criticality), patch, verify. For PHI systems, target critical patches within 30 days. | Vulnerability management procedure, scan reports (Tenable/Qualys/Nessus or equivalent), patch records with timestamps, remediation SLAs |

Recommended approach given your ITIL base: create a vulnerability management practice that feeds into your existing change enablement process. Critical patches become emergency changes; routine patches become standard changes with a defined cadence (e.g., monthly patch Tuesday equivalent).

---

### Incident Management — A.5.24–5.28

You have ITIL incident management, which is a significant head start, but security incident management requires specific additions.

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.24 Planning and preparation | M | Extend your ITIL incident process to explicitly cover security incidents. Define what constitutes a security incident vs. a service incident. | Security incident response procedure, roles defined (including HIPAA breach coordinator) |
| 5.25–5.26 Assessment and response | M | Define classification (P1–P4 or severity tiers) for security incidents. Include PHI breach assessment steps (is this a HIPAA reportable breach?). | Incident classification matrix, response playbooks for top scenarios (ransomware, PHI exposure, credential compromise) |
| 5.27 Learning from incidents | H | Post-incident reviews: document lessons learned and track improvement actions. Auditors look for evidence this actually happens. | Post-incident review reports, corrective action tracking |
| 5.28 Evidence collection | H | Define how to preserve forensic evidence. At minimum: who is authorized to collect logs, chain of custody procedure. | Evidence handling procedure |

---

### Backup and Business Continuity — A.8.13, 5.29–5.30

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.13 Backup | M | Document backup policy: frequency, retention, encryption, offsite/cloud copy, restore testing. EHR backup is likely handled by vendor — get this in writing. | Backup policy, backup job logs, restore test records (at least annual), vendor confirmation of backup arrangements |
| 5.29–5.30 Business continuity | H | Define RTO/RPO for critical systems (EHR especially). Document what happens if the EHR is unavailable (downtime procedures are a HIPAA requirement too). | BCP/DR documentation, RTO/RPO definitions, downtime procedure, test records |

---

### Logging and Monitoring — A.8.15–8.16

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.15 Logging | H | Confirm logs are enabled and retained for: EHR access (PHI audit trail — HIPAA requires 6 years), cloud management plane, network perimeter, authentication systems. | Logging configuration documentation, log retention policy, sample log extracts |
| 8.16 Monitoring | H | Define who reviews what logs, at what frequency. Alert on privileged access, failed authentications, large data exports. | Monitoring procedure, alert configuration, evidence of regular review (tickets, reports) |
| 8.17 Clock synchronization | L | Confirm NTP is configured consistently across all systems. Small thing, auditors do check. | NTP configuration evidence |

---

## Phase 3: Audit Readiness (Months 5–9)

---

### Internal Audit — Clause 9.2

| Action | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Conduct a full internal audit against all Annex A controls in scope and all mandatory clauses. Use a qualified internal auditor (can be staff with training, or an external consultant for first cycle). | Internal audit plan, audit report, nonconformity log |

### Management Review — Clause 9.3

| Action | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Hold a formal management review meeting. Agenda must cover: audit results, risk treatment status, incidents, objectives performance, supplier issues, improvement opportunities. | Meeting minutes, attendance, decisions and action items recorded |

### Nonconformity and Corrective Action — Clause 10.1

| Action | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Document any nonconformities found (internal audit, incidents, supplier issues). Track root cause analysis and corrective actions to closure. | Nonconformity register, corrective action records |

### Stage 1 Audit (Certifier document review)

Schedule with your chosen certification body approximately 1–2 months before your target certification date. They review documentation only. Common failures at Stage 1: incomplete SoA, missing risk treatment plan, no internal audit evidence, scope too vague.

### Stage 2 Audit (Certifier on-site/remote assessment)

Auditors will interview staff, test controls, and sample evidence. Prepare staff in these roles: ISMS owner, IT manager, HR (joiner/leaver process), a clinician (awareness training), cloud/infrastructure lead.

---

## Priority matrix summary

| Priority | Controls / Clauses | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Immediate (Month 1) | Clauses 4–6, SoA, risk methodology, IS policy | Nothing else can proceed without these |
| Month 1–2 | Asset inventory, classification, access control policy, supplier register, MFA | Foundation for everything; highest PHI risk |
| Month 2–4 | Patch management, incident response extensions, logging, backup documentation, cryptography | Likely largest technical gaps |
| Month 4–6 | Physical security docs, BCP/DR, supplier contract review, awareness training records | Important but less likely to block certification |
| Month 6–8 | Internal audit, management review, corrective actions | Mandatory pre-certification steps |
| Month 8–9 | Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits | Certification |

---

## Healthcare-specific notes

A few things that matter more in your context than in a typical organization:

**HIPAA overlap is significant.** Many Annex A controls map directly to HIPAA Technical and Administrative Safeguards. Your SoA justification can note HIPAA alignment, and your existing HIPAA documentation (risk analysis, policies, training records) can serve dual purpose as ISO 27001 evidence. Don't rebuild from scratch — map what you have first.

**PHI data flows need explicit documentation.** Auditors will want to see that you know exactly where PHI is created, stored, transmitted, and disposed of. A data flow diagram covering the EHR, any integrations (labs, payers, referral systems), and staff devices will make this much easier.

**Cloud EHR shared responsibility.** Your EHR vendor's SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certificate covers their controls, not yours. The auditor will ask what you are responsible for — access provisioning, audit log review, configuration of security features — and expect evidence that you are actively managing those responsibilities.

**Downtime procedures** are worth documenting now even if basic. They satisfy both ISO 27001 continuity requirements and HIPAA contingency plan requirements.

### Organization: [Your Organization Name] | Version: 1.0 | Date: [Date] | ISMS Owner: [Name/Role]

---

## How to use this document

The SoA is the central artifact of your ISMS. Every auditor begins here. It must demonstrate that a responsible person made a deliberate, justified decision about every control — not that you implemented everything, but that you thought carefully about what applies and why. Gaps are acceptable at Stage 1; unjustified gaps are not.

**Before your Stage 1 audit, ensure:**
- Every row has a completed justification (not just "N/A")
- Every included control has a named owner
- The document is version-controlled and signed by senior leadership
- It cross-references your risk treatment plan (risks should map to controls)

---

## Document control

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Document title | Statement of Applicability |
| Standard | ISO/IEC 27001:2022 |
| Annex A reference | ISO/IEC 27002:2022 (93 controls, 4 themes) |
| Version | 1.0 DRAFT |
| Classification | Confidential — Internal |
| Approved by | [CEO / COO / CISO] |

| **Remediation action** | Specific next step if not implemented. Must have a target date. |
